title: How do you handle late-arriving / out-of-order data in a streaming pipeline (event-time vs processing-time, watermarks, allowed lateness, windowing), and how do you reprocess historical data (replay from Kafka/object store, backfill jobs, idempotent/exactly-once writes)?
shortTitle: Handling late / out-of-order data and reprocessing in a streaming pipeline
keyPoints: Event-time is when the event actually happened; processing-time is when the engine sees it. Correct streaming uses event-time.
Watermarks are moving markers asserting that all events up to time T have probably arrived, used to trigger window finalization.
Allowed lateness is a grace period after the watermark during which stragglers can still update an already-fired window.
Tumbling, sliding, and session windows bucket an infinite stream into finite computations keyed by event-time.
Reprocessing replays events from the durable log or object store with idempotent writes so re-runs never duplicate.
Keep windowing logic deterministic and version transformations so backfills months later reproduce consistent, auditable results.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use event-time with watermarks and allowed lateness for correct windows despite stragglers, and reprocess by replaying with idempotent writes so re-runs never duplicate.
s1_definition.profdef:
Handling late data and reprocessing involves several cooperating mechanisms.

- **Event-time vs processing-time** – Event-time is when the event happened (carried in the record); processing-time is when the engine sees it. Correct streaming uses event-time.
- **Watermarks** – Moving markers that estimate how far event-time has progressed, used to decide when a window can be finalized.
- **Allowed lateness** – A grace period after the watermark during which stragglers can still update an already-fired window.
- **Windowing** – Tumbling, sliding, and session windows bucket an infinite stream into finite computations.
- **Reprocessing** – Replaying events from the durable log or object store into backfill jobs with idempotent or exactly-once writes.

The goal is correct results despite disorder and safe, reproducible recovery after failures.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India tallies card spend minute by minute, but some slips arrive late from a branch with poor network. Processing-time tallying would wrongly count a 10:00 slip in the 10:05 minute just because it arrived late. Event-time tallying reads the real time stamped on the slip and files it in the correct minute. A watermark is the supervisor saying "I am now fairly sure all slips up to 10:03 have arrived." Allowed lateness is a short grace period to still accept a straggler from 10:02. And if the bank finds a mistake, it re-feeds the stored slips through the counter again with idempotent filing so nothing is double-counted.

sections.s2_detail:
### What is the difference between event-time and processing-time?

Event-time is when the event actually happened, carried inside the record. Processing-time is when the engine happens to see it. In the real world, events are delayed and arrive out of order because of network hiccups, retries, and devices going offline.

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, window, sum as _sum

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("BankEventTime").getOrCreate()

# Each transaction carries its event-time (txn_timestamp)
txns = spark.readStream.format("kafka") \
    .option("subscribe", "bank-transactions") \
    .load()

parsed = txns.selectExpr(
    "CAST(value AS STRING)",
    "CAST(timestamp AS TIMESTAMP) AS kafka_time"  # processing-time
).select(
    col("value").alias("raw"),
    col("kafka_time"),
    # Event-time from the record itself
    col("value").getField("txn_timestamp").cast("timestamp").alias("event_time")
)

# Using event-time ensures a transaction stamped 10:00
# is counted in the 10:00 window even if it arrives at 10:04
```

### How do watermarks work?

A watermark is a moving marker that flows with the stream and asserts: "I believe I have now seen all events with event-time up to T." It is usually derived as the maximum observed event-time minus a bounded-lateness allowance.

```python
# Spark Structured Streaming: 5-second watermark
watermarked = parsed.withWatermark("event_time", "5 seconds")

# Flink equivalent:
# stream.assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(
#     WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
# )
```

```text
Stream of events (event-time → arrival):
  10:00:01 → arrived at 10:00:03
  10:00:02 → arrived at 10:00:05  (out of order)
  10:00:04 → arrived at 10:00:04

Watermark (5s lateness):
  After seeing 10:00:04 → watermark = 10:00:04 - 5s = 09:59:59
  After seeing 10:00:10 → watermark = 10:00:05
  Window [10:00:00, 10:01:00) fires when watermark passes 10:01:00
```

### What is allowed lateness?

Allowed lateness is a grace period after the watermark during which a straggler can still update an already-fired window. After the grace period, very late events are dropped or routed to a side output.

```java
import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.windowing.time.Time;
import org.apache.flink.streaming.api.windowing.assigners.TumblingEventTimeWindows;

// Flink: 1-minute tumbling windows with 30-second allowed lateness
DataStream<TransactionTotal> totals = txnStream
    .assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(
        WatermarkStrategy.<Transaction>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
            .withTimestampAssigner((txn, ts) -> txn.getTimestamp()))
    .keyBy(Transaction::getAccountId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .allowedLateness(Time.seconds(30))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateOutputTag)
    .sum("amount");

// Late events arriving within 30s after window fires: update result
// Late events arriving after 30s: routed to side output for investigation
```

### What are the window types?

Windowing bounds an infinite stream into finite computations. All window types key off event-time so late data lands in the correct window.

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import window, sum as _sum

# Tumbling window: fixed, non-overlapping 1-minute buckets
tumbling = watermarked.groupBy(
    window("event_time", "1 minute"),
    "branch_code"
).agg(_sum("amount").alias("total_amount"))

# Sliding window: 1-minute window every 10 seconds (overlapping)
sliding = watermarked.groupBy(
    window("event_time", "1 minute", "10 seconds"),
    "branch_code"
).agg(_sum("amount").alias("rolling_total"))

# Session window: group bursts separated by 5-minute gaps
# (Flink natively supports session windows)
```

```text
Tumbling (1 min):  |--10:00--|--10:01--|--10:02--|
Sliding (1 min/10s): |--10:00--|
                       |--10:00:10--|
                         |--10:00:20--|
Session (5 min gap): |--burst1--|  gap  |--burst2--|
```

### How do you handle very late data?

Events that arrive after the allowed lateness are dropped by the engine. You can route them to a side output for separate handling or reconciliation.

```java
// Flink: capture very late data in a side output
OutputTag<Transaction> lateOutputTag = new OutputTag<>("late-transactions") {};

SingleOutputStreamOperator<TransactionTotal> result = txnStream
    .keyBy(Transaction::getAccountId)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .allowedLateness(Time.seconds(30))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateOutputTag)
    .sum("amount");

// Process late data separately
DataStream<Transaction> lateData = result.getSideOutput(lateOutputTag);
lateData.addSink(new LateDataSink());  // Write to DLQ or reconciliation table
```

### How do you reprocess historical data?

Because the durable log (Kafka) and the lake (object store) retain events, you reprocess by replaying from a chosen offset or re-reading stored Parquet, then running a backfill job to recompute results for a past period.

```python
# Replay from Kafka at a specific offset for backfill
backfill = spark.read.format("kafka") \
    .option("subscribe", "bank-transactions") \
    .option("startingOffsets", '{"bank-transactions":{"0":1000,"1":2000}}') \
    .option("endingOffsets", '{"bank-transactions":{"0":5000,"1":6000}}') \
    .load()

# Or replay from the lake
backfill_lake = spark.read.parquet("/data/bank/raw/transactions/date=2025-06-*")

# Recompute and write with idempotent upsert
backfill_lake.groupBy("account_id", "txn_date").agg(_sum("amount").alias("total")) \
    .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite") \
    .option("replaceWhere", "txn_date >= '2025-06-01' AND txn_date < '2025-07-01'") \
    .save("/data/bank/gold/account_daily_totals")
```

### Why must reprocessing be idempotent?

Idempotency means re-running the same input produces the same result with no side effects. This is achieved with upserts keyed by a stable event ID, so replaying the same events overwrites rather than duplicates.

```sql
-- Idempotent upsert in Delta Lake
MERGE INTO gold.account_daily_totals AS target
USING backfill_results AS source
ON target.account_id = source.account_id AND target.txn_date = source.txn_date
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET total = source.total
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (account_id, txn_date, total) VALUES (source.account_id, source.txn_date, source.total);

-- Replay produces the same result: no double-counting
```

### What should a senior engineer know?

- Keep windowing logic deterministic and version your transformations so a backfill months later reproduces consistent results. At a bank, corrected figures may feed regulatory resubmissions and must be reproducible.
- The watermark strategy is a tuning decision: too tight drops late data, too loose delays results.
- Session windows are useful for user interaction patterns but complex to implement correctly.
- Spark Structured Streaming and Flink handle watermarks differently: Spark uses a global watermark across all partitions, while Flink uses per-partition watermarks.

```python
# Version your transformation logic for reproducible backfills
TRANSFORM_VERSION = "v2.1"

def compute_daily_totals(df):
    """Deterministic transformation for bank daily totals."""
    return df.groupBy("account_id", "txn_date") \
        .agg(_sum("amount").alias("total")) \
        .withColumn("transform_version", lit(TRANSFORM_VERSION))
```
sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Event-Time vs Processing-Time:

  Real world:    10:00   10:01   10:02   10:03   10:04
  Event occurs:   TXN-A   TXN-B   TXN-C
  Arrives at:     10:01   10:04   10:02
                    │       │       │
  Processing-time:  │       │       │
  Window [10:01]:  TXN-A   │       │
  Window [10:02]:          │     TXN-C
  Window [10:04]:        TXN-B          ← WRONG bucket!
                    │       │       │
  Event-time:       │       │       │
  Window [10:00]:  TXN-A   │       │
  Window [10:01]:          TXN-B   │    ← CORRECT bucket
  Window [10:02]:                TXN-C
```

```text
  Watermark Flow:

  Time ──────────────────────────────────►
  Events:  [10:00] [10:02] [10:01] [10:04]
  Max seen:  10:00   10:02   10:02   10:04
  Watermark:  9:55    9:57    9:57    9:59  (5s lateness)
              │       │               │
              │       │               └─ Window [9:59,10:00) can fire
              │       └─ Window [9:57,9:58) can fire
              └─ Too early to fire any window
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Handling late and out-of-order data starts with computing on event-time instead of processing-time. Event-time is when the event actually happened, and processing-time is just when the engine saw it. Because real-world events are delayed and arrive out of order, aggregating on processing-time puts them in the wrong buckets. Watermarks are the mechanism that decides when a time period is complete: they are moving markers asserting the stream has probably seen everything up to a given time.

When the watermark passes the end of a window, the engine finalizes it, and allowed lateness provides a grace period during which stragglers can still update an already-fired window. Windows themselves bound the infinite stream, whether tumbling, sliding, or session, and they all key off event-time so late data lands correctly.

Reprocessing is the other half. Because the durable log and the lake retain events, you replay from a chosen offset or re-read stored Parquet and run a backfill job. The non-negotiable requirement is idempotency: upserts keyed by a stable event ID ensure re-running neither loses nor double-applies events. At the National Bank of India, this mattered for per-minute card-spend aggregates where swipes arrived out of order from branches with poor connectivity.

Keep windowing logic deterministic and version your transformations so backfills months later reproduce consistent results. In a bank, corrected figures feed regulatory resubmissions and must be auditable.

Remember one sentence: use event-time with watermarks and allowed lateness for correct windows, and replay with idempotent writes for safe reprocessing.
